Steve McQueen's 1-of-10 Ferrari NART Spider Sold for $19M, Is Now the Most Expensive Car He Owned
36 photos
Photo: Christie's
"To me there are cars, and then there is transportation. I don't have a lot of interest in cars that won't go fast and stop well and corner a little. I'd rather sink my fanny into a bucket seat than park it on a bench. I won't sue if you spread the word that I like to drive flat out whenever the road and the law let me." That 1966 Steve McQueen manifesto prints money. Think eight figures.
On November 20, 2026, McQueen's 1967 Ferrari 275 GTB/4 NART Spider headlined Christie's inaugural Rétromobile New York Auctions at Manhattan's Javits Center, and the room responded accordingly. Chassis 10453 hammered at $17,200,000, right inside its $15,000,000 to $20,000,000 estimate.
Add the house's vehicle buyer's premium—12% on the first $250,000 and 10% on the remainder, totaling $1,725,000 in fees—and the final tab hit $18,925,000, making it the priciest Steve McQueen-owned car ever publicly auctioned.
That single gavel drop practically carried the inaugural North American edition of the storied Parisian classic car show on its sculpted Italian shoulders. Across November 20 and 21, 2026, Christie's entire New York sale grossed $51,464,500, meaning McQueen's blue drop-top alone accounted for more than one-third of the event's summed value (36.8%, to be specific). Remarkably, the other nine cars in the top ten combined for $18,965,000, edging out the Spider by just $40,000.
Photo: Christie's Marque loyalists had plenty to cheer about too, with four Ferraris claiming spots inside that ten-car list. Trailing McQueen's star lot were a 1965 Ferrari 275 GTB at $2,205,000, a 1972 Ferrari 365 GTS/4 Daytona Spider at $2,040,000, and a 1965 Ferrari 275 GTS at $995,000. Even the runner-up 1955 Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Alloy Gullwing at $4,735,000 and 1998 RUF Project Dragon at $4,075,000 looked modest beside one of just 10 NART Spiders built.
McQueen's passion for Maranello's four-cam thoroughbred wasn't some impulsive celebrity fling; he had already thrashed a 275 around Riverside Raceway for Sports Illustrated. "I was pushing 140 mph, " he recalled. "Ferrari gearboxes shift like a knife through butter. You throw the stick, and it just kind of finds its own way. " Completed in September 1967 with a 300-hp 3.3-liter Colombo V12, chassis 10453 was invoiced to Luigi Chinetti Motors and delivered through Hollywood Sport Cars.
Though the sixth NART Spider left Italy as the first of only 2 examples painted in Blu Sera over black leather, McQueen wasted zero time making it his own, and immediately had it repainted. He didn’t like the factory shade of blue. Days after his friend Lee Brown finished the makeover, however, a distracted truck driver rear-ended the Spider on Pacific Coast Highway, shoving it into traffic ahead.
Photo: Copyright and Courtesy of Gooding & Company, LLC. Images by Mathieu Heurtault McQueen ordered a replacement coupe, had Junior Conway fix the bodywork, and quietly moved the convertible along by 1971. California engineer J. David Kopf kept the Ferrari for roughly 15 years before Anthony Wang acquired it in 1986, preserving its matching-numbers V12, transaxle, and Scaglietti coachwork for 40 years.
Yet chassis 10453 wasn't the only piece of McQueen history stirring Manhattan bidders. Sold separately right afterward was the car's original factory-issued Bulletin de Garantie (warranty booklet), numbered 2943/1101 and dated October 17, 1967, addressed to Luigi Chinetti Motors in Greenwich, Connecticut.
Safeguarded for decades by a Los Angeles enthusiast who acquired it among McQueen's papers, that humble warranty booklet crossed without reserve against a $10,000 to $20,000 estimate. Collectors promptly lost all composure, bidding the factory slip to $34,375—enough to buy a decent new daily driver.
Combined with the car's $18,925,000 result, the McQueen duo reached $18,959,375, landing just $5,625 shy of outselling the entire rest of the top ten.
Photo: Christie's That frenzy reflects how deeply the King of Cool's fingerprints remain baked into the car itself. When McQueen first inspected the factory Blu Sera finish at Brown's shop, his verdict was instant: "Gotta paint it. Not my kind of blue." He mandated a darker metallic blue respray, ditched the bumpers, added a quick-fill fuel cap, and tapped Tony Nancy to re-stitch the seats—quirks that survived intact alongside Conway's later flared fenders and flip-tail.
With its $18,925,000 auction sale tally, the NART Spider effortlessly shattered the prior public auction record for any car personally owned by McQueen. Until Manhattan, that crown belonged to its own hardtop replacement—the 1967 Ferrari 275 GTB/4 coupe McQueen ordered after his highway shunt, which RM Auctions hammered for $10,175,000 in 2014. Next behind it sat his very first Ferrari, the metallic brown 1963 Ferrari 250 GT Lusso that brought $2,310,000 at Christie's back in 2007.
Completing the five priciest ex-McQueen cars previously auctioned publicly is a trio proving his obsession stretched well beyond Italy. In 2015, Mecum sold his Slate Grey 1976 Porsche 911 (930) Turbo—his final special-order Porsche—for $1,950,000. In 2011, RM Auctions moved his Le Mans-delivered 1970 Porsche 911S for $1,375,000 and his 1953 Siata 208S Spyder, cheekily rebadged with Ferrari emblems, for $946,000.
Photo: YouTube/LexoCars Even the studio-leased $14,080,000 Le Mans Porsche 917K sits behind this Spider. Sure, chassis 10453 stopped well clear of the $27,500,000 model record set by a sister NART Spider in 2013, yet 46 years after McQueen's passing, his aura still commands eight-figure checks without breaking a sweat.
The man who now holds the key s (see the Instagram post below)—and hopefully that $34,375 warranty card—just bought the purest distillation of the man's automotive creed: "They go and they stop and they handle. They are drivers' cars, and most of them have been developed from racing cars."

Officially Saddening: Peugeot Quits WEC, Stellantis' Opel and Citroen Brands Leaving Formula E
7 photos
Photo: Stellantis
Following a Le Figaro report, Stellantis confirmed that it's canning the 9X8 program. The immediate World Endurance Championship exit will be followed by Citroen and Opel pulling out of Formula E after the 2026-27 season, allowing the multinational group created by the merger of PSA and FCA in January 2021 to refocus on customer racing programs and road-going performance models.
Peugeot's departure from endurance racing follows the conclusion of the 2026 season earlier this month. Although the French brand was prepping a revised 9X8 for the 2027 campaign, all that development work has been for nothing . The Citroen and Opel divisions get a little more time in Formula E, for the 2026-27 season finishes in July 2027 with the Tokyo ePrix at the Tokyo Street Circuit.
Looking at the bigger picture, the 9X8 has always been a bit of an unusual proposition. The Lion of Sochaux initially sent its hybrid prototype racer without a rear wing, relying on an outlandish aerodynamic concept that did not work as intended. As such, the 9X8 later gained a rear wing.
All subsequent revisions failed to deliver a competitive breakthrough, and this is part of the reason why the WEC program had to be canned. Four podiums and a lonely pole are the highlights of its five-year campaign, with the works team never winning a race.
Peugeot had a third major upgrade on the menu for the 2027 season, with team principal Emmanuel Esnault promising improvements that would make the 9X8 a regular podium contender. Preps went beyond engineering, with Peugeot already confirming Alex Quinn and Robert Shwartzman for its 2027 driver lineup.
This particularly frustrating development can be explained with numbers. More specifically, the hypercar operation is estimated to cost more than €30 million annually. Stellantis has yet to disclose how much it'll save by leaving the World Endurance Championship.
Photo: Stellantis Although Formula E is losing two Stellantis brands in July 2027, Opel's situation is particularly awkward. Citroen replaced Maserati in the championship, but Opel developed its own Formula E operation around Gen4 regulations. In other words, Opel hadn't even started its Formula E career when the parent company decided that enough is enough.
This, in turn, gives the German outfit a single Formula E season to prove its mettle. Stellantis underlined that its motorsport arm will not be shut down in its entirety. Instead, engineering resources will be moved toward customer racing, with an emphasis on rally cars. Lancia's WRC2 effort comes to mind, a partnership that won the WRC2 teams' championship in 2026.
For some reason, the attached release does not touch upon Lancia Corse HF's 2027 campaign. Be that as it may, its announcement specifically identifies road-going performance models from a total of five brands: Maserati, Alfa Romeo, Lancia, Opel, and Peugeot. Confirmed high-performance monikers include Veloce for Alfa Romeo, GTi for Peugeot , HF for Lancia, and GSE for Opel and its griffin-badged British twin.
Just around 200 people currently working at Stellantis Motorsport will be redeployed into customer racing, performance development, and other activities. Today's decision does not cover Dodge, whose return to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027 remains unaffected. Stellantis North America, which operates as FCA US LLC, directly funds and manages the American brand's NASCAR return.
Dodge exited the Cup Series after the 2012 season finale in November 2012, right after Brad Keselowski won the championship in his Penske Dodge Charger. Instead of building its own engine, Dodge partnered with Earnhardt Childress Racing to supply a rulebook-compliant V8. The naturally aspirated 5.8-liter V8 is capable of making 800 horsepower on short tracks and road courses.

Peninsula Energy says a Nov. 20 cyberattack hit the operating server at its Lance uranium mine in Wyoming. Credit: AdobeStock by terovesalainen
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 23, 2026
Peninsula Energy (ASX: PEN; US-OTC: PENMF) warned Monday that a cyberattack would temporarily disrupt its Lance uranium mine in Wyoming, where low flows from production wells had already forced the company to abandon this year’s output target.
The breach occurred Friday at Lance, about 380 km north of state capital Cheyenne. Peninsula put its recovery plan into effect and asked the Australian Securities Exchange to halt trading. It hasn’t said whether uranium production stopped or how long the disruption might last.
“The cyberattack was on the Lance project’s operating server and system,” CEO George Bauk told shareholders at Monday’s annual meeting. He said the administrative systems at the mine and the corporate office were unaffected.
AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) kept its mines running after it detected unauthorized activity on some of its systems on Oct. 16. The gold miner said in its Nov. 5 quarterly report that it believed it had contained the breach. Industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos tracked 19 ransomware incidents involving mining companies worldwide from July through September. Neither miner has identified the type of attack it faced.
Suppliers hit
Cyberattacks have also hit companies that supply miners. Australian mining software provider Scope Systems offered customers help doing work manually after a May 5 attack encrypted servers it hosted for them. It took until May 17 to restore them all from backups, the company said.
No public evidence links either mining incident to this month’s crippling events in the U.S. involving the FBI’s crime database, Microsoft Outlook email services, the Agriculture Department’s farm loan software, as well as aviation and banking services.
Lance restart
Lance recovers uranium by in-situ recovery, pumping a solution through underground ore and bringing the dissolved metal to the surface. Slow flow rates prompted Peninsula in July to withdraw its 2026 target of 400,000–500,000 lb. of uranium oxide. Before the breach, it was aiming for 500,000–600,000 lb. in 2027.
Workers packed 15,588 lb. into drums in the quarter to Sept. 30, up from 11,482 lb. in the June quarter. Peninsula made no uranium sales in the September quarter. Bauk said Monday the company had about 40,000 lb. in inventory and was waiting for Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) to sign off on product specifications before trucking it off site.
Peninsula shares last traded at A16¢ on Friday, valuing the company at A$91.4 million (C$87 million). The trading halt runs until Peninsula issues an update or trading opens Wednesday, whichever comes first.

Huntington National Bank is challenging former R&R Family of Companies CEO Richard “Rich” Francis’ attempts to protect his multimillion-dollar Florida residence and a collection of other assets from creditors.
The legal battle follows a continuing escalation over the financial fallout from the Pittsburgh-based trucking and logistics company’s collapse in January.
In objections filed Nov. 18 and 19 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Middle District of Florida, Huntington disputed exemptions claimed by Francis for his Marco Island residence, two Pennsylvania properties, a Mercedes-Benz convertible, a Boston Whaler boat, bank accounts and business interests.
Francis valued the Marco Island residence at $8.5 million in his October bankruptcy schedules, although Huntington National Bank has cited a December 2024 appraisal valuing the property at $10.4 million.
The filings come as Huntington has moved a separate lawsuit alleging a fraudulent transfer of Francis’ Florida residence from Collier County Circuit Court into his Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings.
Francis, who formerly headed R&R Family of Companies, filed for personal Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Sept. 22.
R&R’s operations began shutting down in January, leaving hundreds of employees without jobs and carriers and other freight-related businesses pursuing unpaid invoices .
His bankruptcy schedules reported approximately $12.67 million in assets and $7.46 million in liabilities.
Rich Francis and other members of his family are listed as executives of a newly established Pittsburgh-area Giant Logistics LLC , which was organized on Nov. 13, 2025, with an effective date of Jan. 1, 2026, according to Pennsylvania Department of State records.
Huntington targets Marco Island residence
In its Nov. 18 objection, Huntington alleges that R&R Express Properties LLC improperly transferred the Marco Island property to Francis and his wife, Kathleen, while the company was insolvent and heavily indebted to the bank.
Huntington contends the transfer violated R&R’s lending agreements and was intended to place the property beyond the reach of creditors.
The bank’s underlying lawsuit alleges the residence was valued at approximately $10.4 million when it was transferred in December 2025.
Huntington is challenging Francis’ claim that the property, including its improvements and furnishings, qualifies for protection under Florida’s homestead exemption and tenancy-by-the-entireties rules, which can protect certain jointly owned marital property from creditors.
The bank argues that the alleged fraudulent nature of the transfer prevents those protections from applying.
In earlier state-court filings, Richard and Kathleen Francis disputed Huntington’s allegations, arguing that the transaction involved a legitimate mortgage payoff of approximately $5.28 million and that the property was excluded from collateral securing R&R’s broader corporate borrowing.
R&R Express Properties also maintained that Huntington knew about the transaction, supplied mortgage payoff information and received the funds needed to satisfy the loan.
A Florida magistrate recommended Aug. 10 that Huntington’s request to record a lis pendens against the residence be denied. Huntington subsequently filed exceptions challenging that recommendation.
The recommendation was not a final ruling on the fraudulent-transfer allegations.
Bank challenges additional assets
In a second objection filed Nov. 19, Huntington challenged exemptions claimed by Francis for two Pennsylvania properties, including their furnishings, along with a 2018 Mercedes-Benz SL550 and a 2023 Boston Whaler 420 Outrage boat.
The bank also disputed exemptions involving financial accounts, ownership interests in limited liability companies, an interest in the Richard S. and Kathleen L. Francis Revocable Trust, and other assets.
Huntington argues that Francis has not established the legal requirements for holding the disputed assets as tenants by the entirety. It also contends that the existence of at least one joint creditor could make the assets available for administration in the bankruptcy case.
The objections do not establish that Francis concealed assets or committed fraud. Rather, they challenge whether assets disclosed in his bankruptcy proceedings are legally exempt from creditors’ claims.
Property dispute moves to bankruptcy court
On Nov. 17, Huntington removed its Collier County lawsuit to federal bankruptcy court, where it was assigned adversary proceeding No. 2:26-ap-00064-FMR.
The lawsuit seeks relief over the disputed transfer of the Marco Island residence from R&R Express Properties to Francis and his wife shortly before R&R’s operations collapsed.
In the original litigation, Huntington alleged the transfer occurred while R&R was facing significant financial difficulties. The Francises have denied wrongdoing and asserted that their home qualifies for constitutional homestead protection.
Separately, creditor Varilease Finance Inc. has sought additional time to investigate Francis’ claimed exemptions ahead of a scheduled Dec. 10 examination of his financial affairs.
A bankruptcy judge denied Varilease’s agreed extension request Nov. 20 because of missing signature documentation, while allowing the creditor to submit an amended motion.
The court has not ruled on Huntington’s latest exemption objections.
Attorneys for Huntington and Rich Francis did not respond to FreightWaves’ requests for comment.
Why it matters: The outcome of Huntington National Bank’s lawsuit against R&R Family of Companies CEO Richard Francis could determine whether millions of dollars in property and other assets become available to creditors seeking repayment after the collapse of the R&R Family of Companies.

U.S. Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) walks through the U.S. Capitol Building on November 16, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia — The clock has run out on getting lawmakers to back a $350 billion reconciliation bill for the Pentagon, a democratic senator said, likely leaving it to Democrats to sort through the funding mess next year.
“We’re out of time for reconciliation,” Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top democrat on the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee, told reporters here Saturday. “The final bill will be closer to a trillion than $1.5 [trillion]. And at this point, it’ll almost certainly get done next year in a new Congress.”
His comments capped off a week of speculation on Capitol Hill over the state of the administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 ask for the Pentagon. That request revolves around $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a separate reconciliation bill that includes big-ticket items like Golden Dome, drones and multi-year munition buys.
Right now, the clock is ticking on a path ahead. The department is being funded with a continuing resolution that runs out Dec. 11, meaning lawmakers now need to pass another CR or defense spending bill to avoid facing a department shutdown. Democrats are also poised to take the gavels in both chambers on Jan. 3, giving them more power to use the spending bills to cut off funds for the Iran war and reshuffle spending priorities.
But from his perch, Coons urged lawmakers not to wait. Right now, he said, the top priority should be agreeing on topline spending numbers and acknowledging that reconciliation is “dead.”
“If we could get to a bipartisan topline, we could spend the time from Thanksgiving to the end of the year getting a lot of this finished,” he added. “But we still don’t have a topline agreement between the defense and non-defense portions, and that’s the most critical thing now.”
Once that figure is in place, both chambers can continue to refine their respective plans for FY27. In the Senate last week , appropriators released a defense spending bill that centered on a topline of $1.1 trillion. This summer , the House Appropriations Committee released its $1 trillion defense spending bill for FY27. Neither have been approved by the full chamber and could significantly change depending on when the bill is passed and the ultimate topline. From his vantage point, Coons called the Pentagon’s FY27 strategy “sloppy, unprofessional, [and] at times incoherent” since an “enormous” amount of the reconciliation ask should have been requested in the base bill, a move lawmakers are now trying to rectify.
“We have had a good and collaborative bipartisan process between the House and the Senate, the majority and the minority, on moving lots of programs and money [into the base bill],” Coons told reporters. “There is still a fair amount of work to be done.”
When asked about the prospect of forgoing a FY27 defense spending bill and keeping the department at FY26 funding levels via a full-year CR, Coons told reporters that “should not” be the plan.
As lawmakers work through FY27 spending plans, a separate $87.6 billion supplemental request that includes $67.1 billion in defense funds to cover expenses associated with the war in Iran is also withering on Capitol Hill.
Coons said democrats could be on board with passing a version of the request to replenish weapons stockpiles and boost counter-drone defenses if they could ensure the dollars would not be spent to keep the war going.
“My caucus has had the consistent position: Unless there’s an end to this war with Iran, we’re not providing supplemental funding,” Coons added. “There are demonstrable needs … some of us would be willing to fund.”

The Port of Savannah handled 565,366 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, a 25% increase from a year earlier and the second-highest monthly container total in its history.
The October gains pushed container volumes for fiscal 2027 to date up 7.8%, an increase of 152,991 TEUs compared with the same period a year earlier, the Georgia Ports Authority said.
Savannah handled 160 vessels during the month, up 5% year over year.
Container volumes at the global top 30 gateway were driven by strong consumer spending, and an extended peak shipping season, said GPA Chief Executive Griff Lynch, in a statement.
The increase followed September’s 3.7% year-over-year gain, when Savannah handled 504,015 TEUs amid rising imports and weather-related shipment delays.
The cargo gains come as Georgia Ports advances projects designed to expand Savannah’s capacity and improve connections to inland markets.
In October the authority announced a $2.3-billion Savannah Container Terminal investment after receiving a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers . The planned 350-acre facility would provide 3.5 million TEUs of annual capacity, on-dock rail and direct highway access for trucks. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028, and the authority said the completed project would bring Savannah’s total annual capacity to 12 million TEUs.
Separately, the $1.6-billion Ocean Terminal redevelopment is more than 60% complete and will increase the facility’s annual container capacity from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs. GPA said truck gate construction and support services are 99% complete.
FreightWaves previously reported that the Ocean Terminal project’s first container-yard phase is scheduled for completion in mid-fall 2027, with full yard completion targeted for the end of 2028.
The Gainesville Inland Port provides another connection to Savannah, with Norfolk Southern operating direct rail service five days a week between the port and Northeast Georgia. Georgia Ports expects the facility to shift 26,000 containers from highways to rail during its first year.
Suez routing changes could shorten transit times
The return of some ocean carriers to Suez Canal routing is cutting transit times to Savannah by 10 to 12 days as shippers replenish inventory during the holiday shopping season.
The authority also cited improving Panama Canal conditions. The canal authority increased daily vessel transits from 33 to 34 effective Nov. 12 and raised the maximum allowable draft at the Neopanamax locks from 49 feet to 50 feet.
At the Port of Brunswick, total roll-on/roll-off cargo fell 3.6% year over year to 69,599 units in October. Heavy machinery shipments rose 25.8% to 5,193 units, compared with 4,127 a year earlier. Brunswick is the leading East Coast gateway for vehicle imports.
A fourth berth at Brunswick’s Colonels Island facility is 60% complete and scheduled to open in November 2027, according to GPA. The authority said the additional berth will help reduce vessel time at berth and improve cargo flows.
Why It Matters: The October increase means more containers moving through a Southeast U.S. gateway used by importers, exporters, trucking companies and railroads during the holiday shipping period.
